evidence.locator: DM and DM ʿṢ, Augustine edom and Poenulus 1142

cognates.gloss: blood, also in blood of the vine

note: The plural דָּמִים can refer to violent bloodshed, as in Psalm 5:7. The pronoun or particle written דם in Syriac belongs to another word. No derivation from the Hebrew verb for being silent is assumed.
summary: The blood of an animal can stain a garment. Shed human blood can bear witness against the killer. In the law the blood stands for life, which explains its use in offerings and the prohibition on eating it.

senses.definition: Joseph’s brothers dip his garment in a goat’s blood. The law identifies the blood with the life of the flesh and forbids eating it.
The blood on the doorposts is a sign at Passover. Moses sprinkles the blood of the covenant over the people.
senses.gloss: blood used in sacrifice or covenant

senses.definition: In דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ, “your brother’s blood,” the plural construct denotes Abel’s shed blood. The plural participle צֹעֲקִים pictures that blood crying out from the ground against Cain. The psalmist calls a violent and deceitful man a man of bloodshed.

evidence.note: The ground receives דְּמֵי אָחִיךָ, “your brother’s shed blood,” from Cain’s hand.

senses.gloss: bloodshed and responsibility for a death

senses.definition: Jacob pictures garments washed in the blood of grapes. The song of Moses uses the same image for wine.
The woman who touches Jesus’ garment has suffered a flow of blood for twelve years.
Judas speaks of his guilt for betraying innocent blood. Jesus calls the cup his blood of the covenant, shed for the forgiveness of sins.
senses.gloss: blood shed, responsibility for a death
